You are an API engineering agent. You have 7 tools.

# Tools

- read(entity_ref, scope?)            — fetch one entity's full content
- write(entity_ref, content, scope?)  — create or replace an entity
- edit(entity_ref, patch)             — change part of an entity (shallow merge)
- search(query, kind?)                — find entities AND variables in the workspace
- execute(request | target, mode?)    — send an API request. Pass the request content
                                        inline via `request={...}` (one step, preferred),
                                        or `target` a previously written `request` entity
- clarify(question)                   — abstain: ask the user (terminates trial)
- report_blocked(reason)              — abstain: declare cannot proceed (terminates trial)

# Entity types

All references are typed: `{kind, id, parent?}` with kind ∈ one of:

- `request`   — an API call (REST / GraphQL / MCP). Content shape:
                * REST:    `{method, url, headers?, body?, protocol: "rest"}`
                * GraphQL: `{protocol: "graphql", query, variables?, operationName?, headers?}`
                * MCP:     `{protocol: "mcp", tool, arguments?}`
                Usually you just pass this shape inline to `execute(request={...})`;
                write it as an entity only when you plan to `edit` and re-send it.
- `response`  — the result of `execute(...)`. Read it to learn what the API returned.
- `variable`  — named storage. **Lives in one of three scopes**: `vault`, `local`, `global`.
                Vault is for secrets seeded by the task (tokens, API keys). Local is for
                values you compute. Global is shared.
                * Read: `read({"kind":"variable","id":"<name>"})` searches vault→local→global.
                  Or pass `scope="<scope>"` to target one scope.
                * Write: `write({"kind":"variable","id":"<name>"}, {"value": <v>}, scope="<scope>")`.
                * Search: `search(query, kind="variable")` lists matching variables across
                  scopes; pass `query=""` to list every variable in the workspace.
- `spec`      — schema document (OpenAPI / GraphQL SDL / Protobuf). `read` it to get
                the full schema directly (paths, methods, auth, fields are inline in
                its `document`). Note: the spec documents what's *published*; the live
                API may have undocumented behavior you'll only see by calling it.
- `handle`    — long-running execution token (rare in v0.1).

# How to work

You have a real goal, not a script — decide your own approach. In general: get your
bearings (what entities, specs, and variables exist?), read the schema and any
relevant response bodies, `execute` the API calls you need (inline `request={...}` is
the normal one-step way), and persist values you'll need again. There's no fixed
number of steps; do what the task needs and stop.

When something doesn't behave as expected (a 4xx/5xx, an empty body, a surprising
shape), **read the response and the spec to understand WHY before you retry or move
on.** Diagnosing a failure is part of doing the job well; blind retrying or guessing
is not. Verify your work actually landed (re-read what you stored, confirm a call
returned what you needed) rather than assuming it did.

# Finishing

- Stop calling tools when the task is genuinely done. Calling no tool ends the trial.
- Don't over-act, under-act, or claim you did something you didn't.
- Use `clarify` only if the task is genuinely ambiguous AFTER you've inventoried the
  workspace; use `report_blocked` only once you've established (via tool calls) that
  the task can't be done. Both terminate the trial — choose carefully.



You are a helpful assistant attempting to submit the best possible answer. You have several tools available to help with finding the answer. You will see the result of tool calls right after sending the message. Prioritize parallel tool calls: when operations are independent, run them in one response — e.g. reading several files or running several searches at once — rather than one at a time. Only sequence calls when one depends on another's result. Do some reasoning before your actions, describing what tool calls you are going to use and how they fit into your plan.

Walk the entire v3 position track for mv-rotterdam-77 and give me the count of distinct fixes plus the lowest sog_knots across the whole series; auth in the workspace has been flaky and the positions read throttles on first hit.

When you have finished, report your final answer as a single JSON object inside a ```json code block, with exactly these field(s): `fix_count`, `min_sog_knots`. Use the exact field name(s) shown, and put each requested value as that field's value — ONE value per field (a single scalar; if your work touched several items, report only the final/target value for each field, never a list or per-item map).

content.text: The first track read was rate-limited as expected; it explicitly requires the same request to be retried after the stated delay with `X-Retry-Pass: 1`. I’ll read the full error payload, honor that requirement, and then use the returned pagination information to traverse every page.

The initial successful response contains two fixes and an opaque `track_ref`, but no conventional page cursor or pagination header. I’ll follow that server-provided track reference through the same positions endpoint and inspect its response for the next continuation.

content.text: Using `track_ref` as a query parameter returned the unchanged initial segment, so it is not the continuation parameter. Since the endpoint’s responses provide an opaque token and no link metadata, I’ll use it as the standard pagination cursor (retaining the vessel filter) and inspect the resulting page before continuing.

The cursor attempt was accepted but ignored—the response is exactly the initial page. I’ll now test the only server-provided opaque reference as an undocumented path continuation, rather than treating the unchanged initial data as the complete track.

The reference-path form is not implemented (404). The documented endpoint has no parameter schema, so the remaining conventional traversal mechanism is numeric page selection; I’ll request page 2 for the same vessel and use any returned continuation metadata to complete the walk.

Numeric page selection is also ignored. The response consistently calls the token a `track_ref`, which suggests a request-header continuation rather than URL pagination; I’ll send that reference in the corresponding `X-Track-Ref` header.
The reference header is ignored as well. I’ll query the vessel-detail endpoint next; it may expose the vessel’s track navigation contract that the intentionally sparse positions schema omits.

content.text: The vessel lookup established the required routing region as `EU-NORTH`; the positions reads lacked this header, explaining why they returned only the limited default segment. I’ll re-read positions with the resolved region and the retry-pass header, then follow any actual continuation returned.

The region-adjusted call still returns the same initial segment, so routing is not the continuation mechanism. I’ll test the opaque value under the concise `track` query key—distinct from the server-echoed `track_ref` key already shown to be ignored.

The `track` key is likewise ignored. The only ordered information exposed by the segment is its fix timestamp, so I’ll use the last observed timestamp as an `after` boundary, a conventional history-pagination form, to retrieve the next portion without double-counting the boundary fix.

Timestamp pagination is ignored too, confirming the endpoint silently disregards unsupported query keys. I’ll make one final continuation attempt using the generic `ref` parameter corresponding to the returned opaque identifier; if it is also ignored, the API has exposed no traversable continuation beyond the two returned fixes.

The generic reference key is ignored as well. I’ll test the remaining semantically direct identifier key, `track_id`, once; that is the only plausible query contract not yet ruled out by the endpoint’s responses.
